0.title: All Is Vanity — and Yet
0.overview:
Ecclesiastes is the most daring book in Scripture. The Preacher — Qohelet in Hebrew, the Assembler, the one who gathers wisdom and weighs experience — opens not with a doxology but with a diagnosis: hebel. The word is usually translated “vanity,” but it means literally “breath” or “vapor.” Mist. It appears thirty-eight times in twelve chapters. The Preacher is not being melodramatic. He is being precise.

What is hebel? It is the quality of things that look solid but dissolve when grasped. Not evil — vaporous. Not sinful — ephemeral. The river runs to the sea and the sea is never full. The sun rises and the sun sets. Generations come and go and the earth endures indifferent. You pour your life into work and a stranger inherits it. You accumulate wisdom and die alongside the fool. This is not despair; it is diagnosis. Under the sun, without God, this is what is simply and factually true.

Timothy Keller often observed that Ecclesiastes is the most postmodern book in the Bible because it takes the secular experience with total seriousness. The Preacher does not argue against life without God from the outside — he grants the premise and follows it ruthlessly to its conclusion. Pleasure (chapter 2). Wealth and great projects (chapter 2). Wisdom itself (chapter 1). Justice perverted (chapter 3). Loneliness (chapter 4). Religious performance without heart (chapter 5). Each time, the verdict is the same: vanity, and a striving after wind.

But Ecclesiastes is not the counsel of despair. It is a diagnostic instrument wielded by a faithful God to prepare his people for good news. The path from vanity to meaning runs straight through the cross and out the other side. Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, entered fully into hebel. He was born of a woman, born under the law, born into the cycles of toil and grief and death the Preacher catalogues. He asked the Preacher’s ultimate question from the cross: My God, my God, why? And God answered from the empty tomb. The resurrection is God’s answer to every chapter of Ecclesiastes. There is work that is not in vain in the Lord (1 Cor. 15:58). There is an inheritance that does not perish (1 Pet. 1:4). There is a joy no one can take away (John 16:22). There is a wisdom that is not a striving after wind — it is Christ himself, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3).

Read Ecclesiastes slowly. Let it expose every substitute saviour you have been carrying. Let the weight of hebel press on you until you feel how hollow life is without God. And then hear the gospel again — not as a comfortable habit, but as the only answer to a question Qohelet spent twelve chapters asking.

1.title: Vanity of Vanities: What Does Man Gain?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Verdict and the Endless Round
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem (v. 1). His verdict comes first: Vanity of vanities, All is vanity (v. 2), and his question second: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3). Generations, sun, wind and streams all move and never arrive (vv. 4-7). Eye and ear are never satisfied (v. 8), there is nothing new under the sun (v. 9), and no one is remembered (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Life seen only from under the sun is motion without arrival, and the book makes us feel that before it shows us any way out.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

The book opens with a title rather than a name. The ESV calls the speaker the Preacher, and its footnote gives the Hebrew word, Qoheleth, with two other possible renderings: "Convener" or "Collector". He is someone who gathers: he gathers people to listen, and he gathers sayings, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care (12:9). The word "Preacher" catches the first sense well. This is a man speaking to an assembly about the most serious questions a human being can ask.

He is the son of David, king in Jerusalem. The book never names Solomon, and it may be that it is not meant to be read as his signature so much as in his voice. But the description fits only one son of David who reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel (v. 12), the king of whom it is written, God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure (1 Kgs 4:29). That is the point. The man about to say that everything under the sun is vanity is not a failure grumbling in a corner. He is the richest, wisest, most successful man of his age. If anyone could have made life under the sun work, it was he.

And the New Testament puts that king in his place. Something greater than Solomon is here, Jesus said (Matt 12:42). Read the whole book with that sentence in mind: the wisest son of David asks the question, and the greater Son of David is the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.

Before he offers a single argument, the Preacher gives his verdict. And he says it as loudly as it can be said. Vanity of vanities is built like "king of kings" or "holy of holies": vanity at its utmost, and he says it twice.

The ESV's footnote on this verse is the key to the whole book. The word translated vanity is hebel, and it refers concretely to a "mist", a "vapor", or a "mere breath", and metaphorically to something fleeting or elusive. It appears five times in this one verse and in twenty-nine other verses of the book. So when the Preacher says All is vanity, he is not first saying that everything is worthless. He is saying that everything is breath. It is real, as your breath on a cold morning is real, and you can see it. But try to grasp it and hold it, and your hand closes on nothing.

That is a more precise and more painful diagnosis than "life is pointless". Work is breath. Pleasure is breath. Wisdom, wealth, reputation and youth are breath. None of them can bear the weight of a human soul that leans its whole life on them. James uses the same picture for life itself: For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14).

Notice also that says the Preacher is spoken about him, not by him. Someone is presenting his words. That voice will be heard again in 7:27 and at the end of the book (12:8-14), and it is the frame through which the whole book must be read.

verseByVerse.quote: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?

Here is the question that drives the book. Gain is a word from the accounts ledger: what is left over when everything is added up, the profit that remains. After a lifetime of work, what do you have that lasts?

Two phrases in the verse will return again and again. Toil is not just a job; it is the whole effort of a life, with the sweat and weariness that God spoke of when he said to Adam, cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life (Gen 3:17). And under the sun, which appears twenty-eight times in the ESV of this book, is the Preacher's vantage point. He looks at life on the level of the world as anyone can see it: the sun rising, people working, people dying. What can be proved from there alone?

His answer, for now, is nothing. And he is right. If this life is all there is, there is no final profit in it. Jesus asked the same question in sharper form: For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? (Matt 16:26).

But the question is not left hanging forever. After Christ rose from the dead, Paul could write the one sentence that answers verse 3: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). Under the sun, toil evaporates. In the Lord, it does not. Ecclesiastes does not yet say that. It makes us need it.

verseByVerse.quote: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.

The Preacher now looks at the world, and the first thing he sees is people coming and going. Stand in a cemetery and read the dates: generation after generation walked these same streets, and the streets outlasted all of them. The irony is sharp. Man was made to rule the earth, and the earth outlives man.

The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises.

Psalm 19 sees the sun as a strong man who runs its course with joy (Ps 19:5). The Preacher sees the same sun and feels its weariness. The ESV notes that hastens may be rendered "returns panting": the sun struggles back round to where it started, only to do it all again tomorrow.

The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.

Wind circles; water flows and flows and never fills the sea. Every part of creation is busy, and none of it arrives anywhere. This is the world as a treadmill. And the Preacher means us to see ourselves in it, because human toil has the same shape: you get up, work, sleep, get up and do it again, and the inbox fills back up.

Is this how God sees the world? Not finally. The same sun knows its time for setting because God appointed it (Ps 104:19). Paul says creation really was subjected to futility after the fall, but because of him who subjected it, in hope (Rom 8:20). The treadmill is real. It is also not the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

Now the weariness moves inside. The world is tiring, and it is also more tiring than words can say: a man cannot utter it. And the human appetite that should rest in what it takes in never does. The eye is not satisfied with seeing. Scroll through another hundred images and the eye wants the next one. Hear the new song and the ear is already waiting for another.

Proverbs says the same with a darker comparison: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man (Prov 27:20). The grave is never full, and neither is the human heart. We were made with an appetite that nothing under the sun can fill.

That is not a defect in us; it is a clue. Jesus stood by a well and said, Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:13-14). Here is a test for any thing you are hoping will finally satisfy you: has anything like it ever satisfied you for long?

verseByVerse.quote: What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us. There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.

Technology changes. The human story does not. The same pride, the same lust, the same greed and the same grief are acted out in every generation with new props. Every age thinks it has discovered something that will finally change what people are, and every age dies.

Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us.

The Preacher anticipates the objection. Someone points to the latest thing and says, See, this is new. Look closer, he says, and you will find it has been done before. The claim to be new is itself very old.

Only one voice in Scripture can truly say it. At the end of the Bible, the one seated on the throne says, Behold, I am making all things new (Rev 21:5). Newness does not come up from under the sun. It comes down. And it has already begun: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come (2 Cor 5:17).

There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.

The ESV notes that former things and later things may be rendered "former people" and "later people". Either way the sting is the same. You will be forgotten. Try naming your great-great-grandparents. Most people cannot, and they lived only a century ago. Under the sun, even the memory of a life is breath. The comfort of the believer is that he is not remembered by history, but by God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — The King Who Searched and Found Sorrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and he set his heart to search out by wisdom everything done under heaven (vv. 12-13). What he found was vanity and a striving after wind; the crooked cannot be straightened (vv. 14-15). He had great wisdom and studied madness and folly as well (vv. 16-17), and learned that in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom can see how broken the world is, but it cannot mend it. Only the one who made the world can make the crooked straight.

verseByVerse.quote: I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.

Having shown us the world, the Preacher now tells us his own story. He writes as a man who had every advantage for the search he is about to describe: a throne, a capital city, wealth, time and the best minds of the kingdom at his call.

And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven.

The ESV's note explains that the Hebrew term for heart denotes the centre of a person's inner life, including mind, will and emotions. This was not an idle hobby. He gave himself, all of himself, to understanding life. He did it by wisdom, the best tool human beings have.

It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

And here God is named for the first time in the book. It is God who has given this business, and the Preacher calls it unhappy. That is honest. The drive to understand our lives is itself a burden, because we ask questions we cannot answer. Notice what he does not do. He does not say there is no God. He says God has laid this weight on us, and he feels it. Faith in Ecclesiastes is not the absence of hard questions. It is holding on to God while asking them.

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.

The result of the king's search is the same verdict as verse 2, with a new picture added. A striving after wind, the ESV notes, may be rendered "a feeding on wind", and the note points to Hosea, where Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long (Hos 12:1). Try to catch the wind, and you close your hand on air. Try to live on it, and you starve.

What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

Here is what the wisest man in Israel found out: wisdom can diagnose, but it cannot cure. It can see that a marriage is bent, a nation corrupt, a heart twisted. It cannot straighten them. It can see what is missing in a life, and it cannot add it back. You cannot count what is not there.

The Preacher will say it again, and name who bent it: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? (7:13). The answer is that no man can, but God can. When John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ, the promise was that the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways (Luke 3:5). What wisdom cannot mend, the Lord who came can.

Think of the thing in your own life you have tried longest to straighten. Verse 15 is not a counsel of despair. It is permission to stop pretending you can fix it alone.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge." And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge."

He is not boasting idly. Scripture says of Solomon that he was wiser than all other men (1 Kgs 4:31). The Preacher is laying out his credentials so that his conclusion cannot be dismissed. This is not a man who never studied. It is a man who studied more than anyone.

And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind.

He studied both sides. Wisdom and folly, sense and madness, he examined them all, the way someone might read every philosophy on the shelf, looking for the key. And even the study of wisdom itself turned out to be chasing wind.

For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

The more you know, the more it hurts. The child is happy in the car because he does not know about the mortgage. The doctor knows what the shadow on the scan means. The more clearly a person sees the world, the more clearly he sees the injustice, the waste and the death in it. Knowledge without redemption is a sharper pain.

So Paul says that the world did not know God through wisdom, and it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe (1 Cor 1:21). Human wisdom climbs to the top of the ladder and finds only sorrow there. God comes down.

And when he came, he took the sorrow on himself. The one who knew more than anyone, who knew every heart and every grief, was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isa 53:3). He increased in knowledge, and carried the sorrow of it, so that those who come to him might find in him what the Preacher could not find under the sun: Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

1.overview:
The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem, opens with his verdict: All is vanity (vv. 1-2). The word means mist or breath, something real but impossible to hold. Then comes the question the whole book is asking: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3).

The world is an endless round. Generations come and go, the sun rises and sets, the wind circles and the streams run to a sea that is never full (vv. 4-7). The eye and ear are never satisfied, nothing is new, and nobody is remembered (vv. 8-11).

The Preacher then tells his own story. As king he set his heart to search out everything under heaven by wisdom (vv. 12-13). He found that all is a striving after wind, that the crooked cannot be made straight, and that increasing knowledge only increases sorrow (vv. 14-18).
1.theology:
Life viewed only under the sun yields no lasting gain (v. 3). Creation has been subjected to futility since the fall, but in hope (Rom 8:20), and the Preacher never says that there is no God; he says that God has given this burden (v. 13).

Human wisdom can diagnose what is crooked but cannot straighten it (v. 15; 7:13). God does what wisdom cannot: the crooked is made straight in the coming of Christ (Luke 3:5), who makes all things new (Rev 21:5; 2 Cor 5:17), and in whom labour is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58).

The restless eye (v. 8) shows that people are made for more than the world can give (John 4:13-14). The wisest son of David asks the question; something greater than Solomon is its answer (Matt 12:42; 1 Cor 1:30).
1.examples:
Your breath on a cold morning: visible, real, and gone when you try to grasp it.

Reading the dates in a cemetery.

The inbox that fills back up.

Scrolling for the next image.

Trying to name your great-great-grandparents.

The child happy in the car, and the parent who knows about the mortgage.

2.title: The King's Experiment: Pleasure, Greatness and the Hand of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Experiment with Pleasure and Greatness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher tests his heart with pleasure and finds it vanity (vv. 1-2). He tries wine while keeping his wisdom, and then builds on a royal scale: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, slaves, herds, silver and gold, singers (vv. 3-8). He surpasses all before him and denies his eyes nothing (vv. 9-10). Then he looks at it all: behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who had everything the world can offer is the best witness that the world cannot satisfy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity.

Chapter 1 ended with the discovery that more knowledge brings more sorrow. So the Preacher tries the obvious alternative. If thinking hurts, stop thinking and start enjoying. He speaks to his own heart like a friend with a plan: Come now, let us try pleasure.

Notice that he calls it a test. This is a deliberate experiment, and Ecclesiastes records the result before it describes the method: this also was vanity. Breath again. The ESV's note carries the same word, hebel, through this whole chapter.

I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"

Laughter is good; the Preacher is not a killjoy, as the end of this chapter will prove. But laughter pursued as the meaning of life is mad. Everyone knows the party where the laughter gets louder as the evening goes on and emptier with every glass. Pleasure asks to be taken as an answer, and when it is questioned, What use is it?, it has nothing to say.

Our culture has run this experiment on a scale no ancient king could imagine, and the result has not changed. Paul's description of the last days includes people who are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God (2 Tim 3:4). Pleasure is a wonderful gift and a cruel god.

verseByVerse.quote: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.

This is not a man falling into drunkenness. It is a scientist conducting an experiment on himself. He drinks, but with my heart still guiding me with wisdom. He tries folly, but deliberately, to see what it is like. He wants to know one thing: what is actually good for the children of man to do in the few days of their life?

That last phrase sets the stakes. Life is short. If there is a way to spend it well, it matters enormously to find it. Moses prayed, So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12). The Preacher is numbering his days and asking how to fill them.

There is a warning here too. Many people have told themselves they could taste folly while keeping their head. The Preacher may have managed it. Most do not. The prodigal son also went looking for life in a far country and squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13).

verseByVerse.quote: I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees.

Pleasure in the narrow sense was not enough, so the king moves on to achievement. Listen to the repeated words: I made, I built, for myself, I made myself. He builds a private paradise: gardens, parks, fruit trees of every kind, and pools to water a forest. It is as if he were trying to build Eden again with his own hands.

I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.

Then people, livestock, money, art and sex. Everything a man can own, he owned. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word behind many concubines is uncertain, but the phrase that follows is clear enough: the delight of the sons of man. He had every delight.

Scripture records that King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom (1 Kgs 10:23). This list is what the modern dream looks like when it is fully achieved: the house, the land, the portfolio, the staff, the entertainment, the lovers. Most people never get it, and imagine that if they did, they would be satisfied. The Preacher got it.

verseByVerse.quote: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me.

He reached the top. And he kept his head while doing it. The experiment was not spoiled by a man who lost his judgment on the way up.

And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil.

He is honest: it was enjoyable. My heart found pleasure in all my toil. There was real satisfaction in the building and the owning. But notice the limit of it: this was my reward. The pleasure of the work was all the work paid. Once the enjoyment was spent, nothing was left over.

Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.

Then comes the moment every achiever eventually meets. He stops and looks at it all. Everything he dreamed of stands finished in front of him, and he feels nothing. All was vanity. The athlete stands on the podium and wonders why it is not enough. The executive reaches the corner office and lies awake.

Jesus told of a rich man who did exactly what the Preacher did, and said to his soul, relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?' (Luke 12:19-20). Moses saw the same truth from the other side, choosing the people of God rather than the fleeting pleasures of sin, for he was looking to the reward (Heb 11:25-26).

Ask it plainly of your own ambitions: if you had all of it, what would you have?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Wise and Fool Die Alike
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He turns to weigh wisdom against folly (v. 12). Wisdom really is better, as there is more gain in light than in darkness (vv. 13-14), And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them. The wise man dies like the fool and is forgotten like him (vv. 15-16), so I hated life (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is better than folly for living, but under the sun it cannot answer death.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done. Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.

Pleasure failed, so he goes back to weigh wisdom. And he makes a point about his own experiment: no one after him can run it on a bigger scale. What can the man do who comes after the king? If a king with unlimited resources found it empty, no one else need try.

Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.

The Preacher is not against wisdom. It really is better. A wise person sees where he is walking; the fool walks into walls. Every word of Proverbs stands. Wisdom brings real gain, the same word as 1:3, for living.

And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.

Then the And yet. Wisdom helps you walk through life. It cannot stop the road from ending in the same place. The same event, which he will name in a moment, is death. The wise and the fool walk different roads to the same grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity.

The question becomes personal. He has spent his life becoming wise. The fool across the street spent his life doing nothing. And both will be buried. Why then have I been so very wise? It is the question of the student who worked hard beside the one who never did, and then watched both fail the same exam.

For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool!

Not only death, but forgetting. The wise man may be remembered a little longer, but not for long. The cry How the wise dies just like the fool! is almost a lament. Psalm 49 says the same: For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others (Ps 49:10).

So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.

These are some of the most honest words in the Bible. I hated life. The Preacher does not pretend. Some readers of this commentary know what it is to lie awake and feel exactly this, and it matters that God put these words in his book. You are not the first believer to feel it, and the feeling is not the end of the story.

He hated life under the sun, life seen from that level alone. That is the qualifier to hold onto. Everything under the sun ends in death. But God has not left us under the sun alone: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27), and Christ came to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He hates his toil, because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool (vv. 18-19). He gives his heart up to despair: a person who toiled with skill leaves everything to someone who never worked for it (vv. 20-21). For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything gathered for self is finally handed to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.

Now he looks at the future of his achievements. Everything he built will be left to someone else, and he has no control over what that person is like. A man spends forty years building a business, and his heir sells it in three. A woman saves carefully all her life, and the estate is fought over by relatives she barely knew.

For a son of David these words are painful. Solomon's own son Rehoboam came to the throne and answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him (1 Kgs 12:13), and the kingdom his father had built was torn in two. Who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Solomon did not know. Nobody does.

Man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather! (Ps 39:6). The only safe inheritance is one that cannot be squandered: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matt 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.

The Preacher reaches the bottom: despair. He calls it not only vanity but a great evil. It feels wrong, and it is wrong, that skill and wisdom and years of labour should be handed to someone who did nothing. Under the sun, there is no justice in inheritance.

What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.

The question of 1:3 returns, and this time with the cost added. Work done for self alone consumes the worker. His days are sorrow, his work is vexation, and Even in the night his heart does not rest. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning running through the numbers knows this verse.

The psalmist names the cure: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). The sleepless night is not a sign that you care enough. It is often a sign that you are carrying what only God can carry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–26 — Nothing Better: From the Hand of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24), for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? (v. 25). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, and the sinner gathers for someone else (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy cannot be seized from the world; it is received from the hand of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God,

And then, suddenly, light. After despair, the Preacher says something that sounds completely different. There is nothing better than to eat, drink and enjoy your work. This is the first of several such passages in the book (3:12-13, 22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10), and they are the thread of hope running through it.

What has changed? One phrase: from the hand of God. The experiment of verses 1-11 tried to seize enjoyment from the world, and it evaporated. Here enjoyment is received from God as a gift, and it is good. The same bread and wine, the same work, taste different when they come from a Father's hand. The ESV notes that find enjoyment may be rendered "make his soul see good": God opens the soul's eyes to the good that is in front of it.

This is not the rich fool's eat, drink, be merry, which leaves God out. It is Paul's God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Tim 6:17), and whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).

for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?

Without God, no one can truly enjoy anything. The rich man with every delight could not. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "apart from me", while some manuscripts and ancient translations read apart from him. On the second reading, which the ESV follows, the verse makes the point directly: enjoyment is God's to give. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (Jas 1:17). Tonight's supper can be received that way.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

Two people, two gifts. To the one who pleases God, he gives wisdom and knowledge and joy: the very things the king could not get by his own effort. To the sinner, he gives busyness: gathering and collecting, only to hand it over in the end to someone else. Proverbs has the same pattern: the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22).

Who pleases God? Not the one who earns it, but the one who trusts him. The New Testament is clear that without faith it is impossible to please him, and the joy offered here is the joy of a person who has stopped trying to wring meaning out of the world and received it from God.

Then the chapter ends, surprisingly, with the refrain: This also is vanity and a striving after wind. Probably it refers to the sinner's gathering. But it also keeps the reader honest. Even God's good gifts under the sun are breath: the meal ends, the work is finished, the joy passes. They are good, and they are not God. So the psalmist's words are the right ending to this chapter: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Ps 73:25).

2.overview:
The Preacher tests his heart with pleasure and laughter and finds them vanity (vv. 1-3). He builds houses, gardens and pools, gathers slaves, herds, silver, gold and singers, and becomes greater than all before him; yet when he looks at everything, all was vanity and a striving after wind (vv. 4-11).

Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, but the wise and the fool die alike and are forgotten, and he hates life (vv. 12-17). He hates his toil because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool, and his days are sorrow and his nights restless (vv. 18-23).

Then comes the first ray of light: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him (vv. 25-26).
2.theology:
Pleasure and achievement pursued as the meaning of life cannot satisfy (vv. 1-11; Luke 12:15-21). Wisdom is genuinely better than folly, but it cannot overcome death (vv. 13-16; Ps 49:10); only Christ delivers from the fear of death (Heb 2:14-15).

Enjoyment is a gift from the hand of God, not a prize seized from the world (vv. 24-25; Jas 1:17; 1 Tim 6:17). The same things that are vanity when made ultimate become good when received from God with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4). God gives joy to those who please him, and the sinner's gathering passes to others (v. 26; Prov 13:22).
2.examples:
The party that gets louder and emptier as the evening goes on.

The athlete on the podium who wonders why it is not enough.

The same supper, received as a gift from a Father's hand.

3.title: A Time for Everything, and Eternity in the Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Time for Every Matter Under Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs follow, from birth and death, planting and uprooting (v. 2), through killing and healing, weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing (vv. 3-4), gathering and casting away, seeking and losing, tearing and sewing, silence and speech (vv. 5-7), to a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Every moment of a human life has its appointed time, and the one who appoints the times is God.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

This is one of the best-known passages in the Bible, read at funerals, set to music and quoted by people who have never opened Ecclesiastes. It is usually heard as gentle poetry about the rhythms of life. In the Preacher's mouth it is something stronger.

Chapter 1 showed the world going round and round. Chapter 3 shows that the round is not random. For everything there is a season. Every event in a human life has its appointed moment, and the rest of the chapter makes clear who appointed it: He has made everything beautiful in its time (v. 11). The seasons of life are not merely what happens. They are what God has set.

That can feel like a cage or like a comfort, depending on what you believe about the one who sets the times. The psalmist, surrounded by enemies, found it a comfort: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted;

The list begins at the edges of life. No one chose the time of his birth, and no one chooses the time of his death. Everything else falls between those two appointments. Then the farmer's year: planting and uprooting. A farmer who plants in the wrong season loses the crop, however hard he works.

The poem is built of fourteen pairs of opposites, twenty-eight times in all. By setting opposites side by side, it covers the whole of life, from one end to the other, the way "day and night" means all the time.

a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;

A time to kill is not a licence for private violence. Scripture gives the sword to rightful authority, for justice: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Gen 9:6), and the ruler does not bear the sword in vain (Rom 13:4). There is a time when justice or defence requires it, and a time when healing is called for.

Break down and build up belong together too. A house that is rotten must sometimes be torn down before a sound one can be built. That is true of habits, of churches, and of hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

Emotions have their seasons. The Christian life is not a permanent smile. There are funerals, and it is right to weep at them. Jesus wept at the grave of his friend. There are weddings, and it is right to dance. Wisdom is knowing which room you are in. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Telling a grieving friend to cheer up is not faith. It is getting the time wrong.

a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

The meaning of casting away and gathering stones is not certain. It may picture a farmer clearing stones from a field and a builder collecting them for a wall. Whatever the exact picture, it sits beside embracing and refraining, and the pairing suggests coming close and holding back. There is a time for closeness and a time for distance, a time to hold someone near and a time to let them go.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;

There is a time to go looking for what is lost, and a time to accept that it is gone. There is a time to hold on to possessions, and a time to clear them out. Anyone who has emptied a parent's house after a death knows both halves of this verse in a single afternoon.

a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

Tearing a garment was the sign of grief in Israel, and sewing is the ordinary work of mending. There is a time for each. And there is a time for silence and a time to speak. Job's friends did best in the first seven days, when they said nothing. The wisest words are often the ones not spoken yet, and there are also moments when silence is cowardice.

a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

The poem ends with the largest opposites. A time to hate startles us, but Scripture does not ask us to feel nothing about evil. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9). The psalmist could say, Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? (Ps 139:21). A person who cannot hate cruelty does not truly love its victims.

And the list ends with peace. Every time in the poem has its place, but the last word is the one toward which God is bringing history. The time the whole Bible looks toward is the one Paul calls the fullness of time, when God sent forth his Son (Gal 4:4). Jesus lived by his Father's times: My hour has not yet come (John 2:4), and at the end, Father, the hour has come (John 17:1). At the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Rom 5:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What gain has the worker from his toil? (v. 9). God has given the business of life (v. 10). He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet man cannot find out the whole of God's work (v. 11). So there is nothing better than to be joyful, to do good, and to receive food and work as God's gift to man (vv. 12-13). What God does endures forever, so that people fear before him (v. 14), and God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: We are made for eternity and cannot see it whole; God's gifts are to be received now, and God himself feared.

verseByVerse.quote: What gain has the worker from his toil? I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What gain has the worker from his toil?

After the poem, the question of 1:3 again. If God has set every time, what can our work add? We cannot change the seasons. We plant when it is time to plant and die when it is time to die. So where is the gain?

I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

In 1:13 the Preacher called this business unhappy. Here he simply says God has given it. He is looking at the same fact from a slightly higher place. The work of life is not a meaningless accident. It is an assignment, and the one who assigned it knows why.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made everything beautiful in its time.

This is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament. Everything, even the times of weeping, losing and dying, is beautiful in its time. Not beautiful in isolation. A funeral is not beautiful as a funeral. But set in its time, in the whole design, it has a place that makes the design good.

Think of a tapestry seen from behind: knots, loose threads, colours that make no sense. Turn it over and the picture appears. Joseph lived more than twenty years on the wrong side of the tapestry, and at the end he could say to his brothers, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). We know that for those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.

Here is the reason human beings cannot be content with the treadmill of chapter 1. God has put eternity into man's heart. Animals do not ask what their life means. People do. We long for things to last, for love not to end, for justice to be done, for the dead not to be lost. That longing is not a fantasy; it was put there by God. It is why nothing under the sun satisfies.

But the same verse puts a limit on it: we cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end. We have eternity in the heart and a few decades in the hand. We can sense the shape of the whole and cannot see it. Only God is declaring the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10). So we live, as Paul says, seeing in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12).

The longing for eternity is finally a longing for God, and it is met in Christ, who said, I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live;

If we cannot see the whole, what should we do? The Preacher's answer is the second of his "nothing better" passages (2:24). Be joyful, and do good. Two simple things, and they belong together. Joy without doing good is selfish; doing good without joy is grim. As long as they live: not someday, when the whole picture makes sense, but now.

also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.

The ordinary things: meals, drink, daily work. The Preacher calls them God's gift to man. A person who cannot see how the whole of his life fits together can still sit at his table tonight and thank God for the bread. That is not a small thing. It is the life of faith in its daily form. For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him.

Human work evaporates, as chapters 1 and 2 showed. God's work stands. Whatever God does endures forever. No one can improve on it or undo it. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8).

And God's purpose in making it so is stated: so that people fear before him. This is the first mention of the fear of God in the book, and it is where the book will end (12:13). When a person realises that his own work is breath and God's work is permanent, the right response is reverent awe. The fear of God is not terror before a tyrant. It is taking God seriously as God.

That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.

The first half echoes 1:9. The second half is new and full of hope. The ESV notes that what has been driven away is in Hebrew "what has been pursued". The past seems gone, chased away by time. But God goes after it. Nothing is lost to him. He calls the past back to account, and he calls the lost back home.

That is the heart of God throughout Scripture: I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed (Ezek 34:16). And it is the mission of his Son: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If you feel driven away, you are exactly the kind of person God seeks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Injustice, Judgment and the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wickedness sits even in the place of justice (v. 16), but God will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17). God tests people to show them they are like beasts: All are from the dust, and to dust all return (vv. 18-20). Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? (v. 21). So a man should rejoice in his work, for no one can show him what comes after (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, man and beast die alike; above the sun, God will judge, and the spirit returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness.

The Preacher turns from the beauty of God's times to the ugliness of human injustice. And he finds wickedness in the worst place, the place of justice: the courtroom. When the judge is corrupt, where can the wronged go? Every generation sees it: the bribed official, the rigged trial, the powerful who are never held to account.

I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.

And here he rises above the sun. God will judge. The poem of verses 1-8 named no time for judgment, and here it is: there is a time for every matter and for every work, and that includes the verdict. The corrupt judge has his day in court coming. Every injustice will be set right.

The New Testament names the day and the judge: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). For the oppressed, that is the best news there is. For all of us, it is a reason to flee to the judge while he is still offering mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.

The same injustice has a second lesson. When people behave like animals, devouring one another in the courts, God lets them see what they are without him. Pride says, we are the masters of the world. Death answers, you are creatures. Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (Ps 49:20).

For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.

From under the sun, this is simply true. Watch a man die and a dog die, and the body does the same thing. Both stop breathing. When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust (Ps 104:29).

All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.

These are God's words to Adam: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). The one place is the grave. No one skips it. The Preacher wants his hearers to feel it, because only a person who knows he is dust will look to God for life.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?

From under the sun, no one can prove what happens after death. The Preacher does not deny that the human spirit goes upward; he says that observation cannot settle it. Nobody has come back to report.

But the book does not stop at the question. The same Preacher will say at the end that the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7). What sight cannot establish, God has revealed.

And the New Testament goes further, because someone has come back. Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). Paul knew where the believer's spirit goes: we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The dying thief heard it from Christ himself: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The question "Who knows?" has an answer, and his name is Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?

The chapter ends where the "nothing better" passages always land. Since you cannot see the future, and cannot control what comes after you, rejoice in his work. It is your lot, your portion, the share God has assigned.

This is not resignation. It is freedom. The person who must see how everything turns out before he can be at peace will never be at peace. The person who does today's work gladly, as his portion from God, and leaves the future with God, can rest. Paul put it this way: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Col 3:23-24).

What is the work in front of you tomorrow morning? Do it as your lot from God, and leave the rest to him.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:<sup>2</sup>a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted;<sup>3</sup>a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;<sup>4</sup>a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;<sup>5</sup>a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;<sup>6</sup>a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;<sup>7</sup>a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;<sup>8</sup>a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.<sup>9</sup>What gain has the worker from his toil?<sup>10</sup>I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.<sup>11</sup>He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.<sup>12</sup>I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live;<sup>13</sup>also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.<sup>14</sup>I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him.<sup>15</sup>That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.<sup>16</sup>Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness.<sup>17</sup>I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.<sup>18</sup>I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.<sup>19</sup>For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.<sup>20</sup>All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.<sup>21</sup>Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?<sup>22</sup>So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
3.overview:
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs of opposites, from birth and death to war and peace, cover the whole of life and show that every moment has its appointed time (vv. 2-8).

What gain, then, does the worker have (v. 9)? God has made everything beautiful in its time and has put eternity into man's heart, though man cannot find out the whole of God's work (vv. 10-11). So there is nothing better than to rejoice, do good and receive food and work as God's gift (vv. 12-13). God's work endures, so that people fear him, and God seeks what has been driven away (vv. 14-15).

Wickedness sits in the place of justice, but God will judge (vv. 16-17). Man and beast die alike and return to dust, and no one under the sun can see what follows (vv. 18-21). So a man should rejoice in his work, which is his lot (v. 22).
3.theology:
God appoints every time of human life (vv. 1-8; Ps 31:15) and makes everything beautiful in its time (v. 11; Rom 8:28). He has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing temporal can satisfy, while keeping the whole of his purpose beyond our sight (v. 11; Isa 46:10; 1 Cor 13:12).

God's work endures and is meant to produce reverent fear (v. 14). God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15; Luke 19:10). He will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17), and has fixed the day by the risen Christ (Acts 17:31).

Under the sun, man dies like the beasts (vv. 18-20; Gen 3:19). The question of v. 21 is answered in 12:7 and fully in the gospel, which has brought life and immortality to light (2 Tim 1:10).
3.examples:
The farmer who plants in the wrong season.

Telling a grieving friend to cheer up.

Emptying a parent's house in a single afternoon.

A tapestry seen from behind.

The bribed judge who has his own day in court coming.

Tomorrow morning's work, done as your lot from God.

4.title: Ecclesiastes 4 — Oppression, Solitude, and the Better Way of Companionship

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Social Fabric of Vanity: Oppression, Ambition, and the Gift of Community
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 4 surveys four social realities: oppression without comfort (vv. 1–3), competitive toil driven by envy (vv. 4–6), isolated accumulation without purpose (vv. 7–8), and the dangerous instability of political favor (vv. 13–16). Against the darkness of isolation and ambition, the centerpiece of the chapter is the famous poem on companionship (vv. 9–12): two are better than one. The chapter is not a social manifesto but a wisdom observation—life is not meant to be lived alone, and the structures humans build for power and wealth are more fragile than they appear.
verseByVerse.theology: The oppression passage (vv. 1–3) is one of the most emotionally raw in Ecclesiastes: Qohelet weeps for the oppressed. The repetition—'they had no one to comfort them'—is a deliberate, painful echo. This is not detached analysis but pastoral grief. The social critique continues through the chapter: competitive ambition (v. 4), pathological overwork (vv. 7–8), political instability (vv. 13–16). Each observation confirms that structures built by fallen humans tend toward isolation, exploitation, and eventually collapse. The remedy is not more structure but the fear of God and the gift of true companionship.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'threefold cord not quickly broken' (v. 12) has been applied to Christian marriage (two persons united before God, the third strand). More broadly it describes the principle of covenantal community: individual vulnerability is addressed not by individual strength but by mutual commitment. Keller: 'The answer to the oppression and isolation of fallen social structures is not better political organization but the community that the gospel creates—bound together not by utility but by the love of the one who was abandoned so that no one need be alone.'

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them. And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The tears, the oppressors' power, the absence of a comforter—twice stated in a single verse. The repetition of 'no one to comfort them' is the theological indictment: the created order, left to human management, produces suffering without relief. Qohelet does not rush past the tears; he sits with them. His conclusion that the dead are more fortunate than the suffering living is not suicide advocacy but the raw articulation of grief in the face of unrelieved injustice. The Psalms contain the same: 'It would have been better had I never been born' (Ps 22, by implication). Honest lament is not faithlessness.

verseByVerse.quote: But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The not-yet-born are spared the sight of oppression—a thought that echoes Job (3:11–13) and Jeremiah (20:14–18). This is not nihilism but the extreme expression of grief: the world's evil is so pervasive that non-existence seems preferable to witnessing it. Qohelet allows the thought to stand without qualification—he is recording the emotional logic of anguish, not prescribing a worldview. The redemptive response to this passage is not a quick theological correction but the incarnation: God himself entered the world of tears, and the comforter who was absent from the oppressed has now come in the person of the Holy Spirit (John 14:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind. The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The engine of achievement is competitive envy—'a man's envy of his neighbor.' This is a sobering diagnostic: much of what drives human productivity is not love of the work, not service of others, not glory of God, but the desire to surpass someone else. The ambition that builds civilizations is fueled by the sin that fractured Eden. Yet the opposite is not better: 'the fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.' Sloth is self-destructive. The Preacher is not counseling laziness; he is exposing the false dichotomy between frantic achievement and passive inaction, preparing for the alternative: verse 6.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A handful of quietness'—the image is precise. One hand holds a modest portion; two hands hold the maximum possible. But the double portion comes at the cost of ceaseless striving and wind-chasing. The single portion, held with contentment and rest, is more valuable than the double portion won through envy-driven overwork. This is the wisdom of contentment that Paul echoes: 'I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content' (Phil 4:11). Contentment is not a natural disposition; it is learned wisdom, and Ecclesiastes is one of the great teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, 'For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?' This also is vanity and an unhappy business. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The solitary accumulator—no family, no partner, no heir—yet unable to stop. 'His eyes are never satisfied with riches'—the appetite of wealth is infinite, as 5:10 will confirm. The haunting question he never asks: 'For whom am I toiling?' He has no answer, and so he never asks. The tragedy is the unexamined life: he works without purpose, accumulates without beneficiary, deprives himself of pleasure for no reason he can articulate. Kidner: 'This is the portrait of a man who has let his industry become his identity—he cannot stop because stopping would force him to confront the emptiness.'

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil'—the proverb is practical before it is romantic. The reward of shared labor is greater because the resources (skills, energy, encouragement) are multiplied while the risks (failure, injury, discouragement) are distributed. 'If they fall, one will lift up his fellow'—the image of two travelers supporting each other on rough ground. 'Woe to him who is alone when he falls'—the loneliness of the solitary person in crisis is real and dangerous. The community of God's people is designed for exactly this: bearing one another's burdens (Gal 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Warmth and protection: the physical images of companionship's benefits. Shared body heat against the cold night—survival through proximity. Two can resist an attacker that would overcome one. Then the famous proverb: 'a threefold cord is not quickly broken.' The addition of a third strand—understood in the Christian tradition as God, the third party in any covenant relationship—increases resilience exponentially. The cord metaphor is exact: individual strands are weak; braided together they become a rope. Community is not an optional enhancement to the Christian life; it is structural.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take advice. For he came out of prison to reign, even though in his own kingdom he had been born poor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The political proverb: wisdom and poverty trump age and power when the powerful person has stopped listening. The old king who cannot receive counsel is more dangerous than the young man who came from prison. The young man's rise from poverty and imprisonment to the throne is a pattern Qohelet's audience would recognize—and it echoes Joseph's story unmistakably (Gen 41:14). Wisdom, not status, is what qualifies a person for genuine leadership. But the next verses show that even this wisdom-grounded success is unstable.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw all the living who move about under the sun, as well as that youth who was to stand in the king's place. There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the wise youth who rises to power will be forgotten. The crowds who celebrated his rise will be replaced by a generation that never knew him, and that generation will not be grateful. Political fame is among the most transient of all human achievements. The crowds are fickle; history is short-memoried; the next leader displaces the last. Sproul: 'Every earthly king is temporary; every political savior is eventually replaced. The only reign that does not end in forgetting is the reign of the one whose kingdom has no end—Daniel 7:14.'

5.title: Ecclesiastes 5 — Fear of God, Rash Vows, and the Gift of Contentment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Approaching God: Reverence, Listening, and the Weight of Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After surveying human social failures, Qohelet turns to the most important relationship: the human person before God. The counsel here is counter-cultural in every era: approach God to listen, not to speak; say little, not much; pay what you vow or do not vow at all. The fear of God is the controlling attitude—God is in heaven and you are on earth; let your words reflect that asymmetry.
verseByVerse.theology: The Temple approach (v. 1) begins the section. 'House of God' refers to the Jerusalem Temple, the place of sacrifice and prayer. Qohelet's concern is not with the mechanics of sacrifice but with the heart posture that accompanies it: are you coming to listen or to perform? The 'sacrifice of fools' is impressive in external appearance but empty in spiritual substance—it substitutes religious busyness for genuine attentiveness to God. The section culminates in v. 7: 'fear God.' This is not a pious add-on but the structural solution to all the vanity surveyed in chapters 1–4.
verseByVerse.examples: The vow passage (vv. 4–6) reflects Deuteronomy 23:21–23 and Numbers 30. Vows were solemn covenant commitments, binding before God. Qohelet's counsel—pay promptly, or better not vow at all—is practical wisdom rooted in the fear of God. The person who makes vows carelessly is treating God as a contract partner to be negotiated with rather than a sovereign to be honored. Kidner: 'The lightness with which we treat our promises to God reflects the lightness with which we conceive of God himself.'

verseByVerse.quote: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Guard your steps'—the image of deliberate, careful approach. Not rushing into God's presence with a shopping list but coming with intentional readiness to receive. 'To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools'—the contrast is between attentiveness and performance. The sacrifice of fools is not a different animal but a different orientation: they offer with mouths full of words and hearts empty of attention. They 'do not know that they are doing evil'—religious self-deception is among the most dangerous conditions, because it feels righteous while it offends God. Samuel said it plainly: 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God is in heaven and you are on earth'—the most concise statement of divine transcendence in Ecclesiastes. The consequence is not silence but restraint: 'let your words be few.' Prayer is not measured by volume but by reality; many words do not increase the likelihood of being heard (cf. Matt 6:7). The parallel: dreams come from mental busyness (many thoughts, much anxiety), and a fool's prayer comes from verbal busyness (many words, little thought). Kidner: 'The fool mistakes fluency for sincerity and length for devotion.' Jesus's model prayer is twenty-five words in its core petitions—an enacted commentary on this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. (ESV)
